name: K8s CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Forbid — skip-on-overlap, valid only where the job is provably idempotent
reasoning: Structural, not documentary: under Forbid the controller asks only whether an active Job object from this CronJob already exists. If one does it creates no Job — no Pod, no process, no HTTP request. Nothing was sent, so nothing about a request can have changed. kubernetes.io, verbatim 2026-08-17: "Forbid: The CronJob does not allow concurrent runs; if it is time for a new Job run and the previous Job run hasn't finished yet, the CronJob skips the new Job run." The condition in this entry's title is not decoration. The check reads Job status and the clock, never content, so it cannot tell a redundant duplicate from distinct work that happens to overlap — and where the skipped run would have done distinct work, a different amount of thinking happens (zero instead of some), which is this register's own FAIL condition. Kubernetes declines to guarantee the property the pass rests on and puts it on the operator: "A CronJob creates a Job object approximately once per execution time of its schedule... Therefore, the Jobs that you define should be idempotent." So the pass is real and the scope is narrow: it holds for the skipped invocation of a job whose idempotence is established outside Kubernetes, and for nothing else.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — bounded above by the cost of one duplicate invocation per overlap event. A function of job runtime against schedule interval, which is a property of the deployment and not of the mechanism.
telemetrySignal: Observable without reading any request/response payload: compare the CronJob's `.spec.schedule` ticks against its Job object history (`kubectl get jobs` / K8s API audit log / CronJob events). A Forbid skip shows as a schedule tick with no corresponding Job creationTimestamp; a Replace shows as a Job deletion event immediately followed by a new Job creation at the same tick. Purely object-metadata and timing — content-blind.
trap: Time-overlap detection with no content check, sitting on top of Kubernetes' own disclaimer that scheduling is "approximately once" and jobs "should be idempotent". Where that assumption does not hold the mechanism silently drops necessary work rather than saving anything.
settlingExperiment: Point a CronJob's Job at a script that makes a real (cheap) LLM API call, set concurrencyPolicy: Replace, and engineer a tick where the previous run is mid-request when the controller replaces it. Check the provider's usage/billing log: if the killed run's tokens were billed despite its output being discarded, Replace nets a wasted call rather than a saving for that overlap.
crosscheckOverride: The first pass graded "Forbid/Replace" as one PASS_ABSOLUTE row. Adversarial re-read refused the blanket claim on two counts: Forbid's safety rests on an idempotency assumption Kubernetes explicitly declines to guarantee, and Replace fails outright. The row was split — this one carries the scope in its own title, and Replace became a separate FAIL rather than being dropped.

name: K8s CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Replace — kill-and-restart on overlap
reasoning: Replace kills a running Job and starts a fresh one when the schedule ticks during an active run. Kubernetes' guarantee stops at the Pod ceasing to run; nothing retracts a model request that Pod had already dispatched. For any call with real latency — which is most of them, and precisely the ones long enough to trigger an overlap in the first place — the kill lands after the request is in flight, so the provider bills the discarded generation and then bills its replacement. That is more tokens on the wire, not fewer: it fails the bar in the direction opposite to the one it was submitted for. It is here because it arrived bundled with Forbid under a single PASS_ABSOLUTE heading, and a register that quietly drops the half that failed is doing the thing it exists to prevent.
savings: None, and negative in the kill-after-dispatch window — which is the common case for jobs long enough to overlap.
telemetrySignal: Content-blind and observable: a Job deletion event immediately followed by a new Job creation at the same schedule tick, correlated against provider-side usage showing a billed generation with no corresponding completed Job.
trap: Reads as the safer sibling of Forbid because it sounds decisive. It is the more expensive one: Forbid declines to spend, Replace spends twice.
settlingExperiment: Point a CronJob at a job that makes one real, cheap model call. Set concurrencyPolicy: Replace and engineer a tick that lands mid-request. Read the provider's usage log: if the killed run's tokens were billed despite its output being discarded, the overlap cost more than doing nothing.
crosscheckOverride: Split out of the Forbid entry during adversarial review. The first pass had already called Replace "the softer half" in its own reasoning and graded the pair PASS_ABSOLUTE anyway.

name: BullMQ job deduplication (Simple Mode)
reasoning: The mechanism is exactly as documented, and the source bears it out: addStandardJob-9.lua runs deduplicateJobWithoutReplace before storeJob, so a colliding job is never written to Redis and never reaches a worker. But the collision test is `SET deduplicationKey jobId NX` — a caller-supplied string against a caller-supplied string, with zero bytes of the payload in the comparison. It cannot distinguish the same request retried from two different requests that happen to share an id, and BullMQ's own example encourages an arbitrary application-level id (`{ id: 'customValue' }`) rather than a hash of the request. When that invariant breaks the second caller's genuinely different request is discarded and `.add()` resolves to the first job's result: the model never sees the second question and the caller is handed an answer to someone else's, with no error. docs.bullmq.io, verbatim: "as long as the job remains in an incomplete state (neither succeeded nor failed), any subsequent job with the same deduplication ID will be ignored." PASS_ABSOLUTE needs the structural argument to hold as a fact about the mechanism; this one holds only on caller discipline the library neither verifies nor can verify, and its failure mode is a changed product returned as though it were the right one. That is the FAIL condition, not a milder version of it. Repo checks out: taskforcesh/bullmq, MIT, 9,303 stars, pushed 2026-08-17.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED, and not claimable — the prize scales with the caller's true-duplicate submission rate, which BullMQ neither measures nor bounds, and the same mechanism that delivers it silently drops distinct work.
provenance: primary-doc (docs.bullmq.io, plus the library's own Lua source read line-by-line)
telemetrySignal: Observable content-blind at the queue: BullMQ emits a `deduplicated` event per suppression, so a count of those against jobs submitted gives the suppression rate. What it cannot tell you is how many of those suppressions were true duplicates rather than distinct work colliding on an id — which is the number that decides whether this was a saving or a fault.
verifiedAgainst: docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/deduplication (page Last-updated 2026-07-31) and github.com/taskforcesh/bullmq src/commands/addStandardJob-9.lua, includes/deduplicateJobWithoutReplace.lua, includes/storeDeduplicatedNextJob.lua — read 2026-08-17
trap: The docs pitch Simple Mode for "a critical update that should not be repeated if the initial attempt is still in progress" — a critical update, not an identical one. The encouraged usage is per-logical-task ids, which is precisely the usage that makes the guarantee untrue.
settlingExperiment: Reframe the entry to content-derived dedup ids (a hash of the canonicalised request body) and it becomes adjudicable again — most likely CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, since nothing in the library enforces that the id was derived that way. As shipped and as documented, it is not that.
crosscheckOverride: Graded PASS_ABSOLUTE on first pass, on a correct and careful reading of the Lua source. Overruled on the ground the first pass itself surfaced and then set aside as a sizing footnote: the dedup key is content-blind by construction, so "no request was ever sent" is a property of the caller, not of the library.

name: AWS SQS FIFO MessageDeduplicationId
reasoning: AWS states: "If you retry the SendMessage action within the 5-minute deduplication interval, Amazon SQS doesn't introduce any duplicates into the queue." Note where the boundary falls. The client does send the second SendMessage; AWS discards it inside a service the customer cannot inspect. That is the provider's word about the provider's internals — no measurement, and no client-side structural argument of the kind that carries the enqueue-time cases where nothing ever leaves the machine. The register's own rule caps it here, and no counted comparison of SendMessage calls against messages delivered to a consumer was run to lift it. Separately, in explicit-id mode SQS compares only the supplied id string and never the body, so two genuinely different requests sharing an id through a producer bug collapse into one with nothing surfaced to the caller.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — the cost of the suppressed duplicate enqueue, and only where the duplicate was genuine.
provenance: primary-doc (AWS SQS developer guide) — provider assertion about provider-side behaviour
telemetrySignal: Content-blind and countable, though nobody has counted it: SendMessage call count against messages actually delivered to consumers, over a window shorter than the 5-minute dedup interval. The gap is the suppression rate. Running that comparison is what would move this entry off CONTRACTUAL_ONLY.
trap: Reads like the same mechanism as an enqueue-time client-side dedup and is not. There the duplicate never leaves the customer's process and the argument is structural; here it goes over the wire and the argument is AWS's.
settlingExperiment: Send N identical SendMessage calls inside one dedup interval against a FIFO queue and count messages received by the consumer. A measured 1-of-N converts this to a pass; anything else is a finding.
crosscheckOverride: Graded PASS_ABSOLUTE on first pass by treating an AWS documentation sentence as a structural argument. It is not one — the distinction is whether the request leaves the client, and here it does.

name: Team/Enterprise per-seat pricing as the sanctioned alternative to account sharing

A seat holder cannot observe their own queue position or rule out different treatment under contention, which is the same unverifiable preferential-capacity claim that already parks the PTU and reserved-tier entries at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (ids 89, 103, 107, 108, 112, 113).

provenance: primary-doc (claude.com/pricing, read as raw HTML rather than converted markdown)

The "Priority access at high traffic times" row survives in the HTML and vanishes in the conversion, so a sweep that reads converted pages concludes the feature does not exist. Any future sweep adjudicating a pricing or feature-comparison table should fetch it raw.

Adversarial re-read fetched the same page as raw HTML instead of converted markdown and found exactly that description, check-marked, in a Team/Enterprise-scoped table — restoring the verdict the 2026-08-12 brief had given it before the promotion.

name: PromptXRay (karminski) — read-only cache-hit diagnostic
reasoning: The tool's own two files do what they say: gateway.py forwards the client's raw body unmodified. But it forwards it to http://127.0.0.1:7411 — a LiteLLM subprocess runtime.py always spawns, with no code path that reaches the real upstream directly. The body the provider actually receives is rebuilt by LiteLLM's OpenAIGPTConfig.transform_request() (pinned litellm[proxy]==1.91.2), and that function is not a pass-through: it rewrites string-form image_url into dict form, and _handle_pdf_url() fetches a referenced PDF and substitutes re-encoded bytes for the reference before the request leaves the machine. It also strips cache_control breakpoints when the resolved host is openai.com, and gates parameters on whether the model name appears in LiteLLM's hardcoded canonical list — which the self-hosted and OpenAI-compatible endpoints this tool is pitched at will not be in. So for a request carrying a file reference, the model reads different content, not merely different bytes. The README's "never rewrites" is an accurate statement of intent for the code its authors wrote and says nothing about the mandatory hop underneath it.
savings: None — a diagnostic, not a lever. The claim under adjudication was that observing traffic through it is free of side effects, and that is what fails.
provenance: primary-doc (the tool's source, and the pinned dependency's source that actually builds the request)
telemetrySignal: Directly observable and nobody did it: capture the bytes leaving the host and diff them against the bytes the client handed the proxy. Any diff on a plain-text request refutes the claim without argument.
verifiedAgainst: github.com/karminski/PromptXRay at 75ccf503 (repo's only commit, 2026-07-11) — README.md, gateway.py, runtime.py, config.py, litellm_callback.py, pyproject.toml; and raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/v1.91.2/litellm/llms/openai/chat/gpt_transformation.py — read 2026-08-17
trap: The general shape, and the one this register keeps meeting: verifying the files with the project's name on them and treating "reaches an internal URL unmodified" as "reaches the model unmodified", when a separate dependency the project makes mandatory is the thing that builds the outbound request.
settlingExperiment: A live capture on the narrow slice — plain text only, canonical model name, non-openai.com host — could support a qualified PASS_METADATA. The unqualified claim is already refuted and no experiment is needed for that.
crosscheckOverride: The 2026-08-12 brief filed this INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE. The first recovery pass promoted it to PASS_METADATA after reading four files, all inside the repo under review. Adversarial re-read opened the pinned dependency those files hand every request to, and refuted it.

name: gRPC retry throttling (token-bucket retry budget)
reasoning: Mechanism, at the level the client actually executes it: the gRPC client keeps one token_count per server name, starting at maxTokens; every failed RPC costs 1 token, every success refunds tokenRatio. grpc.io: "If the token_count falls below half of maxTokens, retries are paused until the count recovers." Read alone, "paused" sounds like PASS_SCHEDULING — same retry, later. gRFC A6 (github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A6-client-retries.md, "Implemented," last updated 2024-08-23) removes the ambiguity: "If token_count is less than or equal to the threshold... RPCs will not be retried until token_count rises over the threshold" — and explicitly, throttled "retry attempts are canceled and failures returned to the application; hedged requests are also canceled." Nothing is rescheduled. The caller gets an error now instead of a retry that had some nonzero chance of succeeding. The token bucket has no way to tell a retry that was doomed anyway (pure waste, genuinely avoided) from one that would have gone through (service denied, not saved) — it only tracks aggregate recent failure rate. So whenever this mechanism actually does something — outside the trigger window it saves nothing, behaving exactly like plain retry — it is by construction suppressing some calls that would otherwise have completed. That is "a changed product sold as a saving," the bar's own FAIL condition, not a timing artifact. It stops holding as even a candidate for the register's scope at all: Anthropic and OpenAI expose HTTP/REST, not gRPC, so this budget lives inside a gRPC channel neither vendor ever sees or offers — it's only reachable if the customer builds and operates their own gRPC-to-HTTP gateway in front of the vendor's API, making the "provider" here the gRPC project, not a frontier LLM vendor. And even behind such a gateway it is one client process's own aggregate budget per server name — it throttles a single caller's retry storm, not the many-caller thundering herd that register #158 already named as the real, unsolved problem. Both caveats the brief raised survive into this entry; neither is a footnote, both are why the ceiling is low regardless of the verdict letter.
savings: None as a clean efficiency gain. Every dollar it "saves" is a suppressed retry that either would have failed anyway (real waste avoided, size unmeasured — depends on backend failure-rate distribution during the specific outage) or would have succeeded (service denied, not saved, and indistinguishable from the first case by the token bucket itself). Applies at all only behind a self-run gRPC gateway, which the typical hosted-API customer of Anthropic or OpenAI does not operate.
provenance: primary-doc — grpc.io official guide plus the gRFC A6 specification it summarizes (github.com/grpc/proposal), both fetched and cross-checked directly; neither is authored by a frontier LLM provider, since none exposes this surface.
telemetrySignal: Not observable from outside the customer's own process. A throttled retry never leaves the gRPC client, so there is no request on the wire and nothing a provider-side or network-level content-blind audit could see. The only trace is in the customer's own client-side OpenTelemetry metrics (grpc.client.attempt.started flattening while error counts keep climbing) — auditing it requires instrumentation access to the customer's own channel, not the provider-facing wire.
verifiedAgainst: grpc.io/docs/guides/retry/, page footer states "Last modified November 26, 2025"; read 2026-08-17. Cross-checked against github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A6-client-retries.md ("Last Updated: August 23, 2024"); read 2026-08-17.
trap: "Paused" reads as delayed; the spec says canceled. The bucket can't tell a doomed retry from one that would have succeeded, so the "savings" quietly include denied service — and the only two providers in scope don't speak gRPC at all, so the mechanism has almost no floor to stand on before it even gets to that problem.
settlingExperiment: Point a self-hosted grpc-gateway at a backend forced to fail >50% of calls, trip the throttle, and watch grpc.client.attempt.started plateau while the application receives immediate errors with no further attempts recorded — confirms cancellation, not delay, directly from the client's own metrics rather than from the doc's wording.
crosscheckOverride: The 2026-08-12 brief filed this PASS_SCHEDULING, reading "paused" as a deferral. The recovery pass read gRFC A6, which the grpc.io page summarises, and found throttled attempts are cancelled with the failure returned to the application immediately — an outcome change, not a timing one. Demoted by the first pass itself, before any adversarial review.

name: Reservation amortization (pure accounting)
reasoning: Amortization is a Cost Management reporting lens applied after the fact to a reservation/savings-plan purchase already on the books: it re-slices a fixed one-time or monthly payment into daily/monthly amounts and reallocates it across the resources (or PTU deployments) that consumed it, purely for chargeback/showback. It never touches a request — the model reads the identical prompt, the identical model answers, and the identical amount of thinking happens, regardless of which cost metric (Actual vs Amortized) a billing admin later selects in the portal or API. Doc: "Amortization is the process of breaking the one-time cost into periodic costs" and, in a separate paragraph, "Amortized costs are available only for reservations and savings plans" (learn.microsoft.com/.../view-amortized-costs, ms.date 2026-07-17, read 2026-08-17). The same page confirms the bill itself is untouched: the Actual-cost view "shows the purchase as it appears on your bill... You will see the same monthly charge on your invoice as well" — amortized cost is a second lens on the same underlying charge, never a different charge. Applies identically to Microsoft Foundry Provisioned Throughput (PTU) reservations: the dedicated PTU page (.../reservations/microsoft-foundry, same ms.date) has its own "Monthly amortized costs" section doing the identical day-splitting arithmetic on a PTU reservation's fixed monthly cost ($200/31 in May, $200/28 in February) — same mechanism, same non-effect on what's billed or served. Trap: this earns PASS_ABSOLUTE only because zero bytes change on the wire; the moment someone sells "amortize your PTU reservation" as a way to *reduce* spend rather than *time-shift its recognition*, that's exactly the bait the brief flagged — no discount, no different tokens, just a different column in a spreadsheet. It stops holding only if Azure ever let the amortized-cost metric feed back into PTU reservation matching or hourly billing decisions; nothing in either page describes that, and the architecture (Cost Management/Billing API reading post-hoc usage exports) makes it structurally unlikely.
savings: None. Amortization reallocates the timing and resource-attribution of an already-fixed reservation/PTU-reservation payment; it does not reduce what is paid — the invoice total is identical under Actual and Amortized views. (The reservation purchase itself can cut PTU cost vs. hourly pay-as-you-go, per Microsoft's separate PTU reservation pricing material, but that's the discount from *committing*, not a product of amortization, which is a pure reporting/chargeback split of that already-fixed cost.)
telemetrySignal: Not observable at the inference wire, and that's structural, not a gap: amortization is computed after the fact from stored billing/usage-export records inside the Cost Management/Billing API (Actual cost vs Amortized cost metrics, UnusedReservation/UnusedSavingsPlan charge types) — nothing in a chat-completions or PTU-deployment request/response reflects it. A content-blind audit of model traffic would see identical requests, responses, latencies, and token counts whether or not amortization was ever viewed; the only place it's visible is a billing-export diff showing the same total reservation cost reallocated across days/resources, never a change to what was served.
trap: Reads as "amortization saves you money" if the "breaking...into periodic costs" framing is heard as a discount rather than a recognition-timing/chargeback split; the invoice total is unchanged, so any pitch that quantifies "savings" from amortization itself (as opposed to from the reservation purchase decision) is selling a relabeled cost, not a smaller one.
settlingExperiment: Diff PTU deployment inference requests/responses and hourly reservation-matching/billing decisions with Cost Management's metric toggled between "Actual cost" and "Amortized cost" — expect byte-identical inference traffic and identical hourly reservation coverage in both cases, since amortization only reads stored usage/billing records after the fact and writes nothing back into the metering or serving path.

name: Azure PTU Reservations — exit and cancellation mechanics
reasoning:
Mechanism: exit/cancellation terms don't touch what the model reads at all — canceling, exchanging, or holding a PTU reservation changes nothing about the request, the deployment, or the model; it only changes who pays what. So the whole question is a billing-contract fact, not a serving fact. Microsoft's PTU billing doc labels the reservation "Cancelable, with limits | Reservations can be canceled or exchanged after purchase, but those actions might incur fees" (provisioned-throughput-billing, ms.date 2026-05-22 — unchanged since the brief). The general Azure Reservations exchange/refund page supplies the limits (ms.date 2026-07-22, also unchanged): "The total canceled commitment can't exceed 50,000 USD in a 12-month rolling window for a billing profile or single enrollment," and on fees: "We're currently not charging an early termination fee, but in the future there might be a 12% early termination fee for cancellations." (The brief's ETF fragment was a light paraphrase dressed in quotes — this is the verbatim sentence; substance is unchanged.)

Every one of these is a documentation sentence about Microsoft's own billing system — no request was ever sent, nothing measurable, only Microsoft's word that the $50k pool and 12% figure are what actually gets enforced. That caps it at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY by the register's own rule. And here the provider's word isn't even self-consistent: the PTU billing page says exchanges across deployment type "aren't supported... cancel the existing reservation and purchase a new one for the target type and region," while the sibling Foundry-PTU-reservations page (ms.date 2026-07-17) lists "Deployment type: Exchange between Global, Data Zone, or Regional deployment types" as something an exchange can do. Two current, same-vendor Microsoft Learn pages contradict each other on the one mechanic this entry is about — direct evidence that this is provider assertion, not verifiable fact.

Trap / where it stops holding: the $50,000 cap is pooled across the whole billing profile, not per-PTU-reservation — the exchange page's own worked example uses a $108,000 (36-month, $3,000/mo) commitment and shows you can't cancel any of it until you've already paid down to within $50k of the remaining balance. A production-sized PTU commitment can exhaust that shared pool on its own, before counting any other Azure reservations (VMs, SQL, etc.) sharing the same allowance — "cancelable, with limits" can mean "not cancelable for most of the term" in practice. The 12% ETF is explicitly inactive today with "no date" given for enabling it, so this entry only holds until Microsoft flips that switch — at which point exit gets strictly more expensive with no advance-notice commitment stated anywhere in either doc.
savings: None — this is not itself a savings lever, it's the exit-risk characterization of the already-registered PTU-reservation lever (ids 103, 112). The downside it quantifies: the un-refundable portion of a canceled commitment once the shared $50,000/12-month refund pool is exhausted (Microsoft's own example: none of a $108,000 commitment is cancelable until $58,000 has already been paid), plus a reserved-but-inactive 12% early-termination fee that could apply to future cancellations with no stated notice period.
telemetrySignal: Cannot be observed from API/request traffic at all — cancellation status, refund-pool consumption, and any early-termination fee are billing-account and reservation-order facts (Azure Cost Management / Reservations portal, invoice line items), not anything that appears on the wire to the model. A content-blind audit of prompts and responses has no visibility into this; it requires billing/reservation-transaction data instead.
verifiedAgainst: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/concepts/provisioned-throughput-billing (ms.date 2026-05-22; re-read 2026-08-17) — matches brief's cited date exactly, "Cancelable, with limits" row confirmed verbatim; learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/reservations/exchange-and-refund-azure-reservations (ms.date 2026-07-22; re-read 2026-08-17) — matches brief's cited date exactly, $50k/12-month cap confirmed verbatim, ETF sentence confirmed (brief had paraphrased it); cross-checked against learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/reservations/microsoft-foundry (ms.date 2026-07-17; re-read 2026-08-17), which contradicts the first source on whether PTU reservations can be exchanged across deployment type.
trap: A production-sized PTU commitment can exhaust the shared $50,000/12-month refund pool by itself (Microsoft's own $108k/36-month example shows $0 cancelable until $58k is already spent), so "cancelable, with limits" is functionally "not cancelable" for most of a real commitment's term — and Microsoft's own two current docs disagree on whether you can even exchange across deployment type instead of cancelling outright.

name: AWS Bedrock Provisioned Throughput has no exit
reasoning: A Provisioned Throughput purchase with a commitment term is a capacity reservation billed hourly, not a discount you can toggle off when utilization drops. AWS's own docs, re-read 2026-08-17: "1 month – You can't delete the Provisioned Throughput until the one month commitment term is over... Billing continues until you delete the Provisioned Throughput" (prov-throughput.html). The delete page states the same thing more bluntly: "You can't delete a Provisioned Throughput by Model Units with commitment before the commitment term is complete," and "You will still be charged the full provision fee for your current term, whether you run inference or not." It also auto-renews by default at term end — "Your Provisioned Throughput will automatically renew at the end of each commitment term" — unless you act first, so the lock re-arms itself. Exchange is narrow, not absent: base-model PT can't change model at all; custom-model PT can only move to its own base model or a sibling custom model from the same base. No resale/secondary-market path appears anywhere in the purchase/edit/delete flow. This stops being FAIL only for the "No commitment" tier (delete anytime, no discount), or if you cancel auto-renew ahead of term-end on Provisioned Throughput by Tokens — which blocks the *next* term, not the one you're already in. The trap: reading a committed-use discount as insurance you can unwind mid-term; it's a bet that utilization holds for the full term, and AWS re-places that bet for you automatically if you don't cancel it first.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — the per-MU/per-token committed-use discount isn't published as a flat rate (the doc directs you to "contact your AWS account manager" for MU pricing), and realized value depends on utilization: because billing runs the full term regardless of inference volume, an over-provisioned or under-used commitment can turn a nominal discount into a net loss versus on-demand pricing.
telemetrySignal: Observable without reading any prompt content: GetProvisionedModelThroughput exposes commitmentDuration/status fields on the resource itself; Cost Explorer shows a flat hourly Provisioned Throughput line item that doesn't track InvokeModel call volume (billing continues through idle periods); and a DeleteProvisionedModelThroughput call issued before the commitment term ends returns a validation/state error. All three are account- and billing-metadata signals, not model-output signals.
verifiedAgainst: docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html (no revision date shown on page; read 2026-08-17), cross-checked against prov-thru-delete.md, prov-thru-edit.md, and prov-thru-purchase.md on the same domain (all read 2026-08-17)
trap: Mistaking a committed-use discount for a cancel-anytime hedge. It's a bet on sustained utilization for the full term, not insurance against a usage drop — and unless you preemptively cancel auto-renew, AWS re-bets it into another full term for you by default.
settlingExperiment: Not run (would cost real money to prove empirically): purchase a 1-month Model-Units Provisioned Throughput, call DeleteProvisionedModelThroughput on day 2, and confirm it returns a validation/state error rather than succeeding. AWS's documentation states this outcome directly, so the experiment would only be corroborative, not decisive on its own.

name: No EC2-RI-Marketplace-style secondary market exists for LLM capacity
reasoning: This entry isn't a token-mechanism claim — it's a market-existence claim gating every "buy committed LLM capacity, hedge by reselling it later" pitch (Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, OpenAI/Azure committed-throughput). AWS's own eligibility list is the trap-closer: it names exactly one category of thing you can sell — "Only Amazon EC2 Standard regional and zonal Reserved Instances" — then names two more exclusions explicitly, Convertible RIs, and "Reserved Instances for other AWS services, such as Amazon RDS and Amazon ElastiCache." Bedrock Provisioned Throughput was never an EC2 RI to start with, so it isn't merely excluded by that third bullet — it was never a candidate. Same sweep's sibling finding (id 194, re-verified 2026-08-12) already closed the other exit: AWS's own PT docs state the commitment can't be deleted or exchanged before the term ends, only left to run. name: Moonshot/Kimi context caching — no output-invariance statement anywhere in the documentation
reasoning:
Mechanism, at wire level: Kimi's /v1/chat/completions takes `messages` exactly as sent — no cache_id, no TTL field, nothing added to or removed from what the customer writes. Server-side, once a prior request's prompt exceeded 256 tokens, a new request sharing that prefix can have the prefix served from reused KV-cache compute instead of a fresh forward pass; below 256 tokens nothing is cached at all and the request is discarded from consideration. The bytes the model reads are identical either way — what's unstated is whether the *logits* the reused-KV path produces are bit-identical to a fresh pass.

Quote, verbatim, fetched today (both the English page at platform.kimi.ai and its Chinese mirror at platform.kimi.com — which is also where platform.moonshot.cn now redirects, confirming there is one current doc tree, not several): "A new request can hit the prefix cache only when the previous request's prompt tokens exceed 256. If the previous request's prompt tokens are below 256, the request is not cached and is discarded." That sentence, plus one paragraph naming the mechanism as fully-automatic prefix/KV reuse ("no manual creation... no cache ID references... no TTL management"), is the complete extent of what the page says. I read the full page via raw HTML fetch (not the AI-summarized WebFetch pass, to avoid exactly the paraphrase-as-quote trap rule 2 warns about): zero instances of "identical," "unchanged," "same output," "no impact," or any behavior-neutrality language, in either language version.

This is the same feature-class as Gemini implicit caching, register id=93 — and that's not an analogy I'm drawing, it's the register's own real precedent, read directly from strict-verdicts.json: a first reviewer passed Gemini's entry by analogy to Anthropic/OpenAI's explicit invariance statements; a second reviewer re-fetched Google's primary doc, found no invariance sentence there either, and demoted it to INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE under the instruction to default stricter when uncertain. Kimi's page is thinner than the Gemini page that got demoted — Gemini's at least states "we automatically pass on cost savings" and gives per-tier token floors; Kimi's states only the 256-token threshold and punts all pricing to a separate page that itself carries no cache-discount number. There's no basis to sit above where the better-documented, structurally-identical feature landed.

Condition under which this stops holding: a temperature-0 diff — same >256-token prefix sent twice, comparing completion tokens on the guaranteed-miss first call against the likely-hit second call (readable off the response's own `usage.cached_tokens` field, confirmed present in Kimi's live API reference example). That would move this to PASS_ABSOLUTE/PASS_REPLAY on a match or FAIL on divergence. This project holds no Kimi API key and cannot run it — the brief said so and that hasn't changed as of 2026-08-17.

Trap: a plain web search on this topic returns a confident line — "context caching... does not change the model's output quality or response content" — phrased as if it were Kimi's stated policy. The current feature is fully automatic with no client-managed cache object at all; citing the old manual-cache pricing against today's automatic feature would be citing a superseded mechanism.

name: Who captures a mid-term list-price decrease on committed-spend or PTU agreements
reasoning: Two different "committed" mechanisms answer this in opposite directions, and Anthropic doesn't answer it at all — the entry's title bundles all three under one question, but the model reads identical tokens regardless of the answer, so what's being adjudicated is a billing-allocation fact, not a wire-level technique, and the ceiling is the provider's own word. Azure's Enterprise Agreement enrollment pricing (the master committed-spend contract) passes a mid-term list cut straight through: "Microsoft might drop the current Enterprise Agreement price for individual Azure services during the term of an enrollment. We extend these reduced rates to existing customers while the lower price is in effect" — increases are capped at "your price protection ceiling," so the asymmetry favors the customer (learn.microsoft.com/.../manage/ea-pricing-overview, "Price changes"). But a PTU Reservation is a narrower, separately-purchased commitment layered on top of that enrollment, and it works the opposite way: you "purchase the reservation to lock in the discounted rate" (learn.microsoft.com/.../concepts/provisioned-throughput) — fixed for the term at the price in effect on purchase day. A list cut six months into a one-year PTU reservation benefits only new reservations; the customer holding one must proactively cancel or exchange it (refunds capped at $50,000 per 12-month rolling window, term resets on exchange) to reach the new rate. Anthropic's Commercial Terms have neither clause: H.1 gives Anthropic only the unilateral right to update published rates on 30 days' notice ("Anthropic may update the published rates, to be effective the earlier of 30 days after the updates are posted"), with committed-spend pricing itself carved out as "unless otherwise agreed by the parties" — genuinely off-doc, and a full-text search of the document turns up no "commitment," "minimum," "most-favored," "renegotiate," or "price protection" language anywhere. That's exactly where the brief left it, and re-reading confirms it rather than moving it. The trap: reading Azure's EA passthrough clause and assuming it covers the PTU reservation you actually hold — it's the opposite mechanic, opt-in only via exchange, and this stops holding for Azure the moment you're pricing a reservation rather than enrollment consumption, or the moment Microsoft revises the exchange cap or price-protection language. It never holds for Anthropic at all, on the current public document.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — the "prize" is asymmetric and vehicle-dependent, not a passive gain. On Azure EA/Prepayment consumption pricing, the drop is captured automatically with no customer action (size unknowable — depends on future Microsoft list-price decisions). On a PTU Reservation, capturing a drop costs a cancel/exchange transaction inside the $50,000/12-month refund cap, with the term reset on exchange, so the "prize" nets against transaction friction and lost commitment progress. On Anthropic committed-spend, there is no published mechanism at all — whatever a customer captures is whatever their account team concedes, unbenchmarked and undisclosed.
provenance: primary-doc for the Azure findings (both clauses quoted verbatim from live Microsoft Learn pages, independently re-fetched by direct HTTP request, not just an AI summary); primary-doc-confirmed-absence for Anthropic (full text of the Commercial Terms read and searched — the weaker evidentiary class of "the document was read in full and the clause isn't there," not a positive assertion).
telemetrySignal: Azure only, and only from billing metadata, no prompt content involved: an EA customer's effective $/unit rate dropping with no corresponding account transaction would show automatic passthrough; a PTU Reservation's effective rate dropping only in lockstep with a reservation cancel-then-repurchase (or exchange) event, not with the underlying list-price-change date, would show the lock-in mechanic instead. For Anthropic, there is no telemetry signal — no clause exists, so any outcome is a private, unaudited term of a bilateral negotiation and structurally unobservable from outside that account team.
